entities.summary:
Collection of 154 sonnets by William Shakespeare, which covers themes such as the passage of time, love, beauty and mortality.

Shakespeare's sonnets were written primarily in the late 1580s and early 1590s, during a period of significant literary innovation and cultural exchange in England. This body of work showcases Shakespeare's mastery of language, form, and emotional depth, influencing generations of poets and writers to come.

The sonnets also contain personal reflections on love, desire, and loss, as well as philosophical musings on the nature of beauty, aging, and mortality. Many of these themes were resonant with contemporary concerns in England, where the English Reformation had led to a growing interest in classical learning and humanist ideals.

Despite their timeless themes and technical sophistication, Shakespeare's sonnets also reflect the social and cultural context of his time, including the influence of courtly love, aristocratic patronage, and the emerging middle class. This complex interplay of personal, philosophical, and historical factors has made Shakespeare's sonnets one of the most celebrated and studied works in the English language.

In the centuries following their composition, Shakespeare's sonnets have continued to inspire poets, artists, and readers around the world, shaping our understanding of love, beauty, and mortality. Today, they remain a vital part of our cultural heritage, a testament to the enduring power of art to express the human experience.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Shakespeare's Sonnets is the collection of 154 sonnets by William Shakespeare (1564–1616), published in 1609 by the bookseller Thomas Thorpe in a quarto edition (SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS. Never before Imprinted.) — a publication that may not have been authorised by Shakespeare, who apparently did not see the collection through the press. The sonnets are divided into two groups: Sonnets 1–126, addressed to a young man (the 'Fair Youth') whose identity has been endlessly debated (candidates include Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton, and William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke), and Sonnets 127–154, addressed to or about a dark-haired woman (the 'Dark Lady', also unidentified). The collection also contains a dedication to 'Mr. W. H.' (the 'begetter' of the sonnets) whose identity remains one of the great puzzles of English literary history.

The sonnets explore the interlocking themes of love, time, beauty, immortality, desire, jealousy, and artistic creation with a density and psychological complexity unparalleled in the English lyric tradition. Sonnet 18 ('Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'), Sonnet 29 ('When, in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes'), Sonnet 73 ('That time of year thou mayst in me behold'), Sonnet 116 ('Let me not to the marriage of true minds'), Sonnet 129 ('Th' expense of spirit in a waste of shame'), and Sonnet 130 ('My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun') are among the most celebrated poems in the English language. The collection's formal mastery — the English (Shakespearean) sonnet form of three quatrains and a couplet (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG), used to develop and complicate an argument or image — is the definitive expression of the English sonnet.

The Sonnets were largely ignored or embarrassed over in the 18th century (the passionate address to the young man was uncomfortable for later readers) but were reclaimed by the Romantics and have been central to English literary culture since.
